{"kind":"proof","text":"Let
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}0,&0\le x<1,\\1,&x=1.\end{cases}
\]
For every \(x\in[0,1)\), \(x^n\to0\), while \(f_n(1)=1\) for every \(n\). Thus \(f_n\to f\) pointwise. If \((f_n)\) converged uniformly, its uniform limit would necessarily be this pointwise limit \(f\).

Take \(\varepsilon=\tfrac14\). For every \(N\in\mathbb Z_+\), set \(n=N\) and \(x_N=2^{-1/N}\). Then \(x_N<1\), so \(f(x_N)=0\), whereas
\[
f_N(x_N)=\left(2^{-1/N}\right)^N=\frac12.
\]
Consequently,
\[
|f_N(x_N)-f(x_N)|=\frac12>\varepsilon.
\]
Hence no \(N\) satisfies the definition of uniform convergence, and therefore \((f_n)\) does not converge uniformly on \([0,1]\).","reason":"The proof first identifies the unique pointwise limit and then directly negates uniform convergence using a fixed positive epsilon and, for every index threshold, an explicit point where the error remains one half."}
